scenario: A contractor proposes moving the shop's orders, stock and finance tables from Azure SQL to Cosmos DB because the shop is opening in two new countries.
options: Agree: Cosmos DB replicates to any region, so it is the correct home for all data once a business goes international
Push back: those tables depend on joins and transactions, so they stay relational; Cosmos DB fits the catalogue, baskets and sessions that need local reads in every region
Agree, but choose the PostgreSQL API so the existing SQL queries and joins keep working unchanged
Push back: Cosmos DB only supports a single write region, so it cannot help an international shop
explanation: Cosmos DB earns its place for data that must sit close to users in several regions, take extreme write rates, or vary in shape - not for relational data with joins and cross-entity transactions, which it cannot do across items and which costs far more to fake. The PostgreSQL API is a different, distributed-Postgres product rather than a way to run T-SQL joins over JSON, and Cosmos DB does support multi-region writes, so the last option is simply wrong.

scenario: The basket container is provisioned at 400 RU/s. During a promotion the Node API starts logging HTTP 429 responses from Cosmos DB.
stem: What does a 429 mean, and what is the SDK already doing about it?
options: The item exceeded the 2 MB limit; the SDK splits the write across two items automatically
The request rate exceeded the provisioned RU/s for that second; the SDK reads the retry-after header and retries several times before surfacing the error
The consistency level is too strong for the region; the SDK downgrades the read to eventual and retries
The container has run out of storage; the SDK queues the write until the partition is split
explanation: 429 is "request rate too large": you asked for more RU in a second than the container has, Cosmos DB refuses rather than queues, and the SDK retries nine times by default using the retry-after header. An oversized item returns 413, not 429, and Cosmos DB never silently changes your consistency level - both distractors describe behaviour that does not exist.

scenario: A multi-tenant container uses /tenantId as its partition key. The UK tenant holds 95% of the data. The container is at 15% of its provisioned RU/s, yet UK requests get 429s.
options: The container is undersized; doubling the provisioned RU/s will remove the 429s
The UK tenant is a hot partition: throughput is divided across physical partitions, so one busy key value hits its share while the rest sit idle
Session consistency is forcing every UK read to the write region, which throttles them
The indexing policy is rebuilding after a schema change and temporarily consumes the UK partition's RU
explanation: A container's RU/s are spread evenly over its physical partitions, so a key value that attracts most of the traffic exhausts its partition's share while the container as a whole looks nearly idle - the classic hot-partition signature. Doubling throughput is tempting but only raises the hot partition's share a little at double the cost; the real fix is a key with even spread, such as a hierarchical /tenantId then /userId key.

scenario: Ana is designing the shopping-basket container. Baskets are always fetched and updated by the signed-in user, and there are millions of users.
stem: Which partition key should she choose?
options: /userId, because it has high cardinality, spreads evenly and appears in every basket query
/country, because it keeps each region's baskets together and there are only a few values to manage
/createdDate, because new baskets are the busiest and this keeps them in one partition
/status, because most queries filter on whether the basket is active or abandoned
explanation: A good key has many distinct values, spreads storage and requests evenly, and is present as an equality filter in the hottest queries - /userId ticks all three for a basket. /country and /status have a handful of values, so one becomes a hot partition, and /createdDate deliberately concentrates today's traffic into one partition, which is the exact failure you are trying to avoid.

stem: The catalogue is replicated to three regions. A shopper who updates their own basket must see the change immediately, but nobody else needs to; the team also wants to enable multi-region writes. Which consistency level fits?
options: Strong, because it guarantees every read in every region sees the latest write
Eventual, because it is the cheapest and the shopper will see the change within seconds
Session, because it guarantees read-your-own-writes at normal RU cost and works with multi-region writes
Bounded staleness, because it caps the lag at a fixed number of seconds
explanation: Session consistency is the default for good reason: a client always reads its own writes, reads cost normal RU, and it is compatible with multi-region writes. Strong is the tempting choice but it doubles read cost, adds cross-region latency, and cannot be combined with multi-region writes at all; eventual does not guarantee the shopper sees their own change.

scenario: Priya adds Australia East and Ireland as regions on the catalogue account, which runs at 4,000 RU/s manual in UK South, then turns on multi-region writes.
stem: What should she expect on the bill and the SLA?
options: The bill stays roughly the same because replicas share the primary region's throughput, and the SLA rises to 99.999%
Throughput and storage are billed for each of the three regions, roughly tripling the data-store cost, and multi-region writes carry a 99.999% read and write SLA
Only storage is billed per region; throughput is billed once, and the SLA remains 99.99% regardless of regions
The bill triples and the SLA falls, because more regions mean more replication conflicts
explanation: Every region holds a full copy of the container and bills its own throughput and storage, so three regions is three bills - and finance should see that multiplier before the tick boxes are ticked. In exchange, a multi-region-writes account carries a 99.999% SLA for reads and writes; the single-region figure is 99.99%, and conflicts are resolved by policy rather than reducing the SLA.

scenario: The team needs the product search index to reflect catalogue changes within seconds, without adding a second write path to the Node API.
options: An Azure Function triggered by the catalogue container's change feed, which receives each insert and update in order
A timer-triggered Function that runs a cross-partition query every 10 seconds for items with a recent _ts
A Cosmos DB stored procedure that calls the search service after each write
Setting TTL on the catalogue container so stale index entries expire automatically
explanation: The change feed is exactly this: a per-container, ordered log of inserts and updates that a Functions trigger consumes without touching the API's write path. Polling with a cross-partition query is the tempting alternative but fans out to every physical partition each run and bills for each; stored procedures are scoped to one partition and cannot call external services, and TTL deletes items rather than syncing anything.

scenario: The production basket container idles at about 300 RU/s overnight and peaks at around 3,500 RU/s during evening promotions.
options: Manual provisioned throughput at 3,500 RU/s, because production must never receive a 429
Autoscale with a maximum of 4,000 RU/s, so the container scales between 400 and 4,000 RU/s and bills the peak each hour
Serverless, because paying per RU consumed is always cheapest for variable traffic
Manual provisioned throughput at 400 RU/s, relying on the SDK's retries to absorb the evening peak
explanation: Autoscale is built for this shape: set a maximum, Cosmos DB scales between 10% and 100% of it, and although the per-RU rate is about 1.5x manual you pay for the peak hour rather than for 3,500 RU/s all night. Manual at 3,500 pays for idle capacity most of the day, serverless is single-region with capped burst throughput and is meant for dev, test and low-traffic apps, and manual at 400 would simply throttle the promotion.
